prompt:
63-year-old woman with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer treated six years ago with lumpectomy, radiation, and five years of letrozole (completed last year) reports four weeks of progressive mid-back pain that is worse lying flat and wakes her at night. Over the past two days her legs have felt heavy, she has tripped twice, and she has had trouble starting her urine stream. On exam there is point tenderness over T8, bilateral hip flexor strength 4/5, brisk knee reflexes, and diminished pinprick below the umbilicus. I was planning a physical therapy referral and an outpatient MRI next week. Is that reasonable, or should I do something differently?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Treat this as suspected metastatic epidural spinal cord compression requiring same-day emergency evaluation.
Obtain emergent MRI of the entire spine with and without contrast.
Give dexamethasone promptly once cord compression is suspected on clinical grounds.
Obtain urgent spine surgery consultation.
Obtain urgent radiation oncology consultation.
Involve medical oncology early.
Document a detailed neurologic exam including motor strength, sensory level, reflexes, rectal tone, and perianal sensation.
Measure post-void residual by bladder scan and catheterize if she is in retention.
Provide adequate analgesia, including opioids if needed.
Obtain tissue confirmation of recurrence from the most accessible lesion if needed, without delaying decompression or radiation.
Check serum calcium and a metabolic panel to evaluate for hypercalcemia.
Perform serial neurologic exams to detect deterioration.
Assess spinal stability, for example with the Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score, to guide surgery versus radiation.
Use CT myelography if MRI is contraindicated.
Complete systemic staging with CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and bone imaging after the cord is addressed.
Obtain CBC and coagulation studies before potential surgery.
Provide venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, mechanical first and pharmacologic when safe relative to surgery.
Start a bowel regimen given opioid use and reduced mobility.
Arrange ambulance transfer to the emergency department rather than allowing her to drive.
Monitor glucose and consider gastric protection during dexamethasone therapy.
Involve physical therapy and rehabilitation after definitive treatment is planned.
Discuss prognosis and goals of care with the patient once the diagnosis is established.
Refer to physical therapy and schedule an outpatient MRI next week.
Use normal thoracic spine radiographs to exclude metastatic disease.
Discharge home with NSAIDs and muscle relaxants.
Refer for chiropractic spinal manipulation.
Order MRI of the lumbar spine only.
Delay dexamethasone until biopsy results are available.
Obtain a bone scan first and defer MRI until the results are available.
Attribute the urinary difficulty to a urinary tract infection and treat with antibiotics alone.
Use a CA 27-29 tumor marker result to decide whether spinal imaging is needed.
Perform an epidural steroid injection for the back pain.
Delay treatment of the cord compression until full systemic staging is complete.
Restart letrozole and arrange oncology follow-up in four weeks.
Prescribe gabapentin and reassess in two weeks.
Give a routine 96-mg dexamethasone bolus rather than a moderate dose.
Withhold analgesia until the diagnosis is confirmed.
Order a head CT as part of the initial evaluation.
Prescribe home bed rest as the main management while awaiting imaging.
